rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Dhu al-Nun” is Jonah: al-nun means the fish, and an informative epithet is preferable to an empty title when its descriptive benefit is clear.
rows.anchor: لا خلاف في أن ذا النون هو يونس عليه السلام لأن النون هو السمكة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas places the fish episode before Jonah’s mission: after resisting a king’s assignment, Jonah was cast from a storm-tossed ship, swallowed unharmed, and later sent to Nineveh, whose people repented and were spared.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنه : كان يونس عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pre-mission chronology is supported by al-Saffat, which says Jonah was cast ashore, recovered, and then sent to a hundred thousand or more.
rows.anchor: ودليل هذا القول قوله تعالى في سورة الصافات : { فنبذناه بالعراء وهو سقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An additional version of the pre-mission account says Gabriel ordered Jonah to warn Nineveh; when Jonah asked for a mount, Gabriel said the matter was too urgent, and the story then follows the ship and fish episode until Jonah is cast at Nineveh.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا القول رواية أخرى وهي أن جبريل عليه السلام قال ليونس عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second chronology puts the fish after Jonah preached to Nineveh and warned of punishment: when punishment was lifted after their repentance, he left them angry.
rows.anchor: أما القول الثاني : وهو أن قصة الحوت كانت بعد دعائه أهل نينوى وتبليغه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reasons proposed for Jonah’s departure after the Ninevites’ reprieve are shame among people who had experienced him as a liar, fear of their custom of killing liars, wounded pride, or anger that punishment had not come.
rows.anchor: وثانيها : أنه كان من عادتهم قتل الكاذب . وثالثها : أنه دخلته الأنفة

rows.speaker: أكثر العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars hold that Jonah’s departure in anger and the fish episode occurred after God had sent him to the people and after their punishment was lifted.
rows.anchor: وأكثر العلماء على القول بأن قصة الحوت وذهاب يونس عليه السلام مغاضبا بعد أن أرسله الله تعالى إليهم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس والحسن والشعبي وسعيد بن جبير ووهب وابن قتيبة ومحمد بن جرير
rows.claim: Most exegetes, including the named authorities and authors selected by the source, are said to read Jonah as having gone away angry at God; proponents of prophetic sin treat that as a grave offense.
rows.anchor: قول ابن مسعود وابن عباس والحسن والشعبي وسعيد بن جبير ووهب واختيار ابن قتيبة ومحمد بن جرير

rows.speaker: القائلون بجواز الذنب
rows.claim: The proponents argue that if Jonah’s anger was directed at God it was a grave sin, while anger at the king or people would still be prohibited, as they read the warning against imitating Jonah.
rows.anchor: احتج القائلون بجواز الذنب على الأنبياء عليهم السلام بهذه الآية من / وجوه

rows.speaker: القائلون بجواز الذنب
rows.claim: They argue that “he thought We would not be able” implies Jonah doubted God’s power.
rows.anchor: احتج القائلون بجواز الذنب على الأنبياء عليهم السلام بهذه الآية من / وجوه

rows.speaker: القائلون بجواز الذنب
rows.claim: They take Jonah’s confession of wrongdoing as an admission of sin, noting that the Qur’an uses “wrongdoers” as a term of blame.
rows.anchor: احتج القائلون بجواز الذنب على الأنبياء عليهم السلام بهذه الآية من / وجوه

rows.speaker: القائلون بجواز الذنب
rows.claim: They argue that, if Jonah had not sinned, God would not have punished him by casting him into the fish’s belly.
rows.anchor: احتج القائلون بجواز الذنب على الأنبياء عليهم السلام بهذه الآية من / وجوه

rows.speaker: القائلون بجواز الذنب
rows.claim: They cite the description of Jonah as “blameworthy” in another passage: a person deserving blame must have sinned.
rows.anchor: احتج القائلون بجواز الذنب على الأنبياء عليهم السلام بهذه الآية من / وجوه

rows.speaker: القائلون بجواز الذنب
rows.claim: They infer guilt from the command not to be like Jonah: they argue that forbidding imitation only makes sense if his conduct was sinful.
rows.anchor: احتج القائلون بجواز الذنب على الأنبياء عليهم السلام بهذه الآية من / وجوه

rows.speaker: القائلون بجواز الذنب
rows.claim: They infer from the contrast with the resolute messengers that Jonah was not one of them, and invoke statements about Moses and the Prophet’s instruction not to rank him above Jonah; al-Razi says this last point is outside the verse’s exegesis.
rows.anchor: احتج القائلون بجواز الذنب على الأنبياء عليهم السلام بهذه الآية من / وجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects anger directed at God: the verse does not identify its object, and a prophet could not be angry with his Lord, since that would imply ignorance of God’s sovereignty and negate faith.
rows.anchor: لكنا نقطع على أنه لا يجوز على نبي الله أن يغاضب ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports that Jonah left over preparations or voluntary worship cannot describe a prophet disobeying a divine command; the Qur’an says believers have no choice against God and His Messenger’s decision.
rows.anchor: وأما ما روي أنه خرج مغاضبا لأمر يرجع إلى الاستعداد ، وتناول النفل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since Jonah’s anger could not be against God, he most likely left angry at his people, the king, or both; his departure angered the people because they feared punishment would descend after he left.
rows.anchor: وجب أن يكون المراد أنه خرج مغاضبا لغير الله ، والغالب أنه إنما يغاضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects that leaving the people was itself forbidden: Jonah was commanded to deliver the message, not to remain with them forever, and the command did not require repeated delivery.
rows.anchor: فإن الله تعالى أمره بتبليغ تلك الرسالة إليهم ، وما أمره بأن يبقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s anger was not a sin: before it was forbidden, he could think it permitted, and it arose from zeal for God, religious honor, and hatred of unbelief; still, he should have endured and waited for permission to migrate.
rows.anchor: من حيث إنه لم يفعله إلا غضبا لله تعالى وأنفة لدينه وبغضا للكفر وأهله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi explains the warning not to imitate Jonah as God’s way of granting Muhammad the highest and best station.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال تعالى : { ولا تكن كصاحب الحوت } كأن الله تعالى أراد لمحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes “naqdira” as “constrain”: Jonah thought God would not restrict his choice to stay or leave. Al-Razi treats this as an excuse, not deliberate disobedience, since he thought the timing was open though delaying was better.
rows.anchor: لن نضيق عليه وهو كقوله تعالى : { الله يبسط الرزق لمن يشاء من عباده ويقدر }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation treats the phrase as a simile: Jonah’s state resembled that of someone who thinks he may leave his people without waiting for God’s command.
rows.anchor: أن يكون هذا من باب التمثيل بمعنى فكانت حالته ممثلة بحالة من ظن أن لن نقدر عليه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة والضحاك والكلبي ورواية العوفي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi, and al-Awfi’s report from Ibn Abbas take “naqdira” to mean “decree”; al-Farra and al-Zajjaj choose this sense, deriving it from measuring or determining something.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مجاهد وقتادة والضحاك والكلبي ، ورواية العوفي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز والزهري وعبيد بن عمير ويعقوب
rows.claim: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and al-Zuhri read the verb with a rounded nūn and doubled consonant; Ubayd ibn Umayr has a doubled passive form, while Yaqub reads a light passive form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر بن عبد العزيز والزهري : ( فظن أن لن نقدر عليه بضم ) النون والتشديد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says Ibn Abbas told Muawiya that the verse uses qadar in the sense of decree, not qudra in the sense of power, resolving Muawiya’s concern that it attributed doubt to a prophet.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما هذا من القدر لا من القدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation uses “be able” figuratively for “do”: ability and action are related, so one may stand for the other.
rows.anchor: فلا يبعد جعل أحدهما مجازا عن الآخر

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd reads the words as a reproachful question: “Did he think We would not decree against him?”
rows.anchor: أنه استفهام بمعنى التوبيخ معناه أفظن أن لن نقدر عليه عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Jonah’s episode preceded his prophethood, the thought may have occurred through Satan’s suggestion before he was a prophet; such a possibility does not apply after his mission.
rows.anchor: على قول من يقول هذه الواقعة كانت قبل رسالة يونس عليه السلام كان هذا الظن حاصلا قبل الرسالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the confession predates prophethood, no reinterpretation is needed; afterward, its surface sense would make a prophet deserving of a curse, so al-Razi takes it as Jonah having left what was better despite being able to do better.
rows.anchor: لوجب القول بكون النبي مستحقا للعن ، وهذا لا يقوله مسلم ، وإذا وجب التأويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fish episode was a trial, not punishment, because prophets cannot be punished; many commentators call any harm connected with a sin a punishment.
rows.anchor: أنا لا نسلم أن ذلك كان عقوبة إذ الأنبياء لا يجوز أن يعاقبوا ، بل المراد به المحنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “blame” attached to Jonah was for leaving the better course, not for a grave sin.
rows.anchor: أن الملامة كانت بسبب ترك الأفضل

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf explains “the darknesses” as the dense darkness inside the fish’s belly, comparing the Qur’an’s use of darknesses elsewhere.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) في الظلمات أي في الظلمة الشديدة المتكاثفة في بطن الحوت

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some interpreters count different layers of darkness: at night, night, sea, and fish belly; by day they add the fish’s intestines.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من اعتبر أنواعا مختلفة من الظلمات فإن كان النداء في الليل فهناك ظلمة الليل والبحر وبطن الحوت

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Other proposed explanations are that another fish swallowed the fish holding Jonah, or that the fish’s deep descent left darkness layered above it.
rows.anchor: أو أن حوتا ابتلع الحوت الذي هو في بطنه ، أو لأن الحوت إذا عظم غوصه في قعر البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Jonah’s fish descended to the seventh earth needs a report to support it; if it is proposed only to explain the darknesses, the other explanations suffice.
rows.anchor: فإن ثبت ذلك بخبر فلا كلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase can be understood as “that there is no god but You,” or as an explanatory “that is to say.”
rows.anchor: فالمعنى بأنه لا إله إلا أنت ، أو بمعنى أي

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to have said that no distressed person who supplicates with this prayer fails to receive a response; al-Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : ( ما من مكروب يدعو بهذا الدعاء إلا استجيب له )

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says God rescued Jonah only because Jonah admitted his own wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن : ما نجاه الله تعالى إلا بإقراره عن نفسه بالظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Glory be to You” declares God free of every defect, including incapacity; it shows Jonah did not mean that God lacked power, but affirmed that God acted with rightful wisdom rather than injustice, vengeance, or inability to free him.
rows.anchor: فهو تنزيه عن كل النقائص ومنها العجز ، وهذا يدل على أنه ما كان مراده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah says he wronged himself by fleeing his people without permission; as a penitent and remorseful person, he asks for the trial to be lifted, as the following verse says God answered him.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى ظلمت نفسي بفراري من قومي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative reading pairs God’s complete lordship with Jonah’s human weakness and shortcoming in fulfilling the right of lordship; that contrast itself suffices as a supplication.
rows.anchor: وهو أنه عليه السلام وصفه بقوله

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf parses “first creation” as the object of “We restore,” with the simile particle absorbed by “as”: God restores the first creation as He began it. The indefinite singular pictures creatures one by one; “creation” is a verbal noun and has no plural.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) رحمه الله : { أول خلق } مفعول نعيد الذي

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One account of resurrection says God separates bodily parts without annihilating them, then reconstructs them.
rows.anchor: فمنهم من قال : إن الله تعالى يفرق أجزاء الأجسام ولا يعدمها ثم إنه يعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says God annihilates bodies completely and recreates those same bodies; al-Razi says the verse supports this because it compares resurrection to the first creation, which is existence after nonexistence rather than assembly of separated parts.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية دلالة على هذا الوجه لأنه سبحانه شبه الإعادة بالابتداء

rows.speaker: القائلون بالمذهب الأول
rows.claim: Supporters of bodily parts remaining extant cite the folded heavens and the transformed earth as evidence that the relevant created parts persist.
rows.anchor: واحتج القائلون بالمذهب الأول بقوله تعالى : { والسماوات مطويات بيمينه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A promise upon Us” can be an emphatic verbal noun, since “We restore it” already states a promise of restoration.
rows.anchor: أما قوله تعالى : { وعدا علينا } ففيه قولان : أحدهما : أن وعدا مصدر مؤكد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the promise is binding because God informed of it and knows it will occur; whatever God knows will occur necessarily does so.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد حقا علينا بسبب الإخبار عن ذلك وتعلق العلم بوقوعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We will surely do it” confirms that the promised resurrection will happen without fail.
rows.anchor: أي سنفعل ذلك لا محالة وهو تأكيد لما ذكره من الوعد

rows.speaker: حمزة والباقون
rows.claim: Hamza reads “al-zubur” with a damma on zāy; the other readers use a fatha. Both readings mean the book.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة بضم الزاي والباقون بفتحها يعني الزبور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root zabara means to write; “mazbūr” is the plural of zubr, and al-zabūr is a book, like the forms “al-halūb” and “al-rakūb.”
rows.anchor: يقال : زبرت الكتاب أي كتبته والمزبور بضم الزاي جمع زبر كقشر وقشور

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد والكلبي ومقاتل وابن زيد
rows.claim: These authorities take the “Zubur” as revealed books and the “Remembrance” as the heavenly Mother Book, where future events are written for the angels and from which prophetic books are copied.
rows.anchor: وهو قول سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد والكلبي ومقاتل وابن زيد الزبور هو الكتب المنزلة

rows.speaker: قتادة والشعبي
rows.claim: Qatada and al-Shaʿbi identify the Zubur as the Qur’an and the Remembrance as the Torah.
rows.anchor: وثانيها : الزبور هو القرآن والذكر هو التوراة وهو قول قتادة والشعبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view makes the Zubur David’s Psalter and the Remembrance something reported from David: “God existed and nothing was with Him, then He created the Remembrance.”
rows.anchor: وثالثها : الزبور زبور داود عليه السلام ، والذكر هو الذي يروى عنه عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s own fourth view takes “the Remembrance” to mean God’s knowledge: God wrote this in the Zubur after already knowing it without forgetfulness, so His promise must occur.
rows.anchor: وعندي فيه وجه رابع : وهو أن المراد بالذكر العلم أي كتبنا ذلك في الزبور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة والسدي وأبو العالية
rows.claim: These authorities take the earth as Paradise and the righteous servants as believers who obey God: God recorded that the righteous will inherit Paradise, citing the blessed inheritance of the Garden and the post-resurrection context.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما ومجاهد وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة والسدي وأبي العالية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة والسدي وأبو العالية
rows.claim: Their argument is that Paradise is specially intended for the righteous, while the unrighteous have a place there only as dependents; worldly earth is shared by righteous and unrighteous, and the verse follows resurrection.
rows.anchor: وأما ثانيا : فلأنها الأرض التي يختص بها الصالحون لأنها لهم خلقت ، وغيرهم إذا حصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed report describes Paradise’s earth as white and pure in support of interpreting “earth” as the Garden.
rows.anchor: فقد روى في الخبر أنها أرض الجنة فإنها بيضاء نقية

rows.speaker: الكلبي وابن عباس في بعض الروايات
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and some reports from Ibn Abbas take the earth as the worldly earth, which God will make believers inherit; they cite the promise of succession and Moses’ statement that God gives the earth to whichever servants He wills.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الكلبي وابن عباس في بعض الروايات ودليل هذا القول قوله سبحانه : { وعد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view identifies the earth as the Holy Land, citing the inheritance of the lands blessed around it; ultimately Muhammad’s community inherits it when Jesus son of Mary descends.
rows.anchor: وثالثها : هي الأرض المقدسة يرثها الصالحون ، ودليله قوله تعالى ؛ { وأورثنا القوم

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf treats “that” as the predicate of an omitted subject, “the matter is this”; it is a transition like a writer’s phrase when turning to a new topic.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) { ذالك } خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي الأمر والشأن ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ḥurma is something whose violation is forbidden; God’s sacred ordinances may mean all obligations or specifically those connected with pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: والحرمة ما لا يحل هتكه وجميع ما كلفه الله تعالى بهذه الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam lists five sacred things: the Kaaba, Sacred Mosque, Sacred City, sacred month, and sacred site.
rows.anchor: وعن زيد بن أسلم الحرمات خمس : الكعبة الحرام والمسجد الحرام والبلد الحرام

rows.speaker: المتكلمون
rows.claim: The theologians say that supererogatory acts are not included among God’s sacred ordinances.
rows.anchor: وقال المتكلمون ولا تدخل النوافل في حرمات الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Honoring God’s sacred ordinances benefits the person because they must be observed and protected; “with his Lord” points to stored reward, not good already received.
rows.anchor: أي فالتعظيم خير له للعلم بأنه يجب القيام بمراعاتها وحفظها

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm explains that honoring the sacred ordinances is better than treating them lightly.
rows.anchor: قال الأصم فهو خير له من التهاون بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because a pilgrim might suppose that consecration forbids livestock along with game, God clarifies that livestock remains lawful except for the prohibitions recited in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: فقد كان يجوز أن يظن أن الإحرام إذا حرم الصيد وغيره فالأنعام أيضا تحرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After praising respect for sacred ordinances, the verse commands avoiding idols and false speech because monotheism and truthful speech are the greatest good; shirk is itself a form of falsehood.
rows.anchor: أتبعه بالأمر باجتناب الأوثان وقول الزور . لأن توحيد الله تعالى وصدق القول أعظم الخيرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command means avoiding idol worship, the chief form of falsehood, and avoiding every kind of false speech rather than approaching any of it.
rows.anchor: فكأنه قال فاجتنبوا عبادة الأوثان التي هي رأس الزور ، واجتنبوا قول الزور كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling idols rijz does not mean they are physically impure: avoiding them is more emphatically required than avoiding filth, and their worship is worse than contact with physical impurity.
rows.anchor: وسمى الأوثان رجسا لا للنجاسة ، لكن لأن وجوب تجنبها أوكد من وجوب تجنب الرجس

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm says idols were called rijz because people customarily spilled blood over them as offerings; al-Razi calls this explanation far-fetched.
rows.anchor: قال الأصم إنما وصفها بذلك لأن عادتهم في المتقربات أن يتعمدوا سقوط الدماء عليها وهذا بعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers the alternative explanation that idols are called rijz to disparage and belittle them.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه إنما وصفها بذلك استحقارا واستخفافا وهذا أقرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From idols” explains or specifies rijz, like “twenty of dirhams”: because rijz is broad, the phrase means the filth that consists of idols, not that only some idols are rijz.
rows.anchor: بيان للرجس وتمييز له كقوله عندي عشرون من الدراهم لأن الرجس لما فيه من الإيهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zūr derives from deviation or turning aside, just as ifk derives from turning someone away.
rows.anchor: والزور من الزور والإزورار وهو الانحراف ، كما أن الأفك من أفكه إذا صرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation of false speech is the fabricated claim that something is lawful or unlawful.
rows.anchor: أحدها : أنه قولهم هذا حلال وهذا حرام وما أشبه ذلك من افترائهم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet, after the dawn prayer, stood facing the people, declared false testimony equal to associating partners with God, and recited this verse; al-Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( أنه صلى الصبح فلما سلم قام قائما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations of false speech are lying and slander.
rows.anchor: وثالثها : الكذب والبهتان

rows.speaker: أهل الجاهلية
rows.claim: The pre-Islamic pilgrimage chant counted as false speech because it affirmed a partner for God while claiming that God owned that partner and whatever it owned.
rows.anchor: ورابعها : قول أهل الجاهلية في تلبيتهم لبيك لا شريك لك إلا شريك هو لك

none: Qur’an text only, quoting the following verses without commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises success to those who combine seven qualities; the segment begins explaining those qualities with “the believers.”
rows.anchor: حكم بحصول الفلاح لمن كان مستجمعا لصفات سبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Qad” contrasts with “lammā”: it affirms an expected event, here the believers’ anticipated glad tidings that success is firmly theirs.
rows.anchor: فقد تثبت المتوقع ولما تنفيه ولا شك أن المؤمنين كانوا متوقعين لمثل هذه البشارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falāḥ means attaining one’s desired end, or remaining in good; aflaha can mean entering success, as abshara means entering glad tidings, or it can be causative, “he made him succeed.”
rows.anchor: الفلاح الظفر بالراد وقيل البقاء في الخير ، وأفلح دخل في الفلاح كأبشر دخل في البشارة

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: Talha ibn Musarrif read aflaha in the passive; a further form aflaha is attributed to him either by the “akalūnī al-barāghīth” dialect or by an indefinite verb followed by an explanatory subject.
rows.anchor: وعليه قراءة طلحة بن مصرف أفلح على البناء للمفعول ، وعنه أفلحوا على لغة أكلوني البراغيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the explanation of faith has already been given in Surat al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم القول في الإيمان في سورة البقرة
